name: Pochvennichestvo
summary: Pochvennichestvo, 'native soil' thought, was the programme of the Dostoevsky brothers' journals Vremya and Epokha in the early 1860s. It held that Peter's reforms had split the educated estate from the common people and that Russia should reconcile the two by returning the educated to the people's native soil, building its own forms of life while keeping European learning, without the enmity of estates seen in Europe, and it put mass literacy first.

keyWorks.title: Two Camps of Theorists (Two Camps of Theoreticians)

evidence.quote: considered from the viewpoint of pochvennichestvo (native soil) position of the publications. The stance of their editorial board is formulated in the Announcement about the publication of the Vremya journal in 1861, which became a program document. The main concept of Vremya, as well as the Epokha journal that followed it, was the need to merge the educated part of society with the people. There was a spiritual, political and social gap, a split between them, which was caused not only by the church reform of the 17th-century, but also by subsequent state reforms that caused people’s rejection. The idea of the Dostoevskys’ journals was to get to know the people, recognize their originality, appeal to the native principle, pochva (soil), the communal form of life, the synthesis of the ideas developed in Europe, which will find their development in the Russian narodnost’ (Russian people). These thoughts were absorbed by F. M. Dostoevsky’s idea of enhanced knowledge of Russia, which was reflected in his article “Two Camps of Theorists.”

Dostoevsky founded, along with his brother Mikhail, the journal Vremya (Time) promoting pochvennichestvo , or the “native soil” movement ( pochva the Russian for soil).

 Dostoevsky’s Russian nationalism was without chauvinism, however, Scanlan claims. Russians had debated their particular role in the world for decades before Dostoevsky, though he addressed the wrestling match between Westernizers and Slavophiles in the 1862 essay, “Two Camps of Theoreticians.”

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki rejected a separate legal status for the gentry, saying it had no foundation in Russian history, and held that 'the gentry was to enjoy neither legal nor institutional distinctions'; Dostoevsky envisaged an order of 'best men' open to anyone, 'not a privileged caste'.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki accepted modern innovations (railways, fire insurance, science in agriculture) but held that 'change was inevitable and desirable but was legitimate only when it took place within the constraints of tradition' and that a sudden, rapid transformation would destroy what was quintessentially Russian. They did not argue about technological speed itself.

bound-labor.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki greeted Emancipation as an event greater than Peter's reforms, and 'came out flatly against the determination of the government to tie the peasants to the land by the terms of the Emancipation settlement', arguing for 'the free movement of labour'.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki shared the 'impulse' of Russian conservative romantics who 'despised capitalism as much for its bourgeois values and life-style as for the suffering it visited on the working man in the West'; Vremia 'deplored the egoism and narrowness of the bourgeois ideal'; Dostoevsky 'returned [from Europe] highly critical of the bourgeois-capitalist society'. They did favour technology (railways, science applied to agriculture), but nothing credits capitalism itself as progressive.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Dowler: 'publicity (glasnost'), by which they meant freedom of speech, of the press, and of conscience, was essential' to the pochvenniki; Strakhov's summary lists freedom of thought and of speech among the principles they supported. Vremia fought the censors. Nothing is said about censoring art for moral reasons specifically.

character-from-environment.rationale: Yang: 'Dostoevsky has always opposed artistic utilitarianism and the formula "the environment is stuck" [sredа zaela]. He feared that the spread of the formula ... would lead to an emptiness of the inner world of a person and a lack of faith.' He rejected environment as the source of character.

class-collaboration.rationale: The manifesto says development must not rest on enmity of estates, with victors and vanquished as in Europe; this is stated of estates rather than employers and workers, so the answer is medium and mild.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki held that Russian nationality 'transcended class interests and hostilities' (Dostoevsky: 'Every Russian is first of all a Russian and after that he belongs to a class') and that Russia's history had militated against Western-style separate estates; they saw progress as the unfolding of the national moral ideal. The sources do not argue the general claim about history, hence -1. Manifesto (Vremia, 1860/61): 'Not enmity of the estates, of victors and vanquished, as everywhere in Europe, must lie at the foundation of the development of the future principles of our life. We are not Europe, and with us there will not and must not be victors and vanquished.'

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Dowler: Vremia's Proudhon-inspired commentary said Russians 'should not be charmed by the allure of wealth' and that 'the proper end of man was spiritual satisfaction and not material prosperity'; articles deplored 'the egoism and narrowness of the bourgeois ideal' and its poshlost'.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki saw the commune as 'the institutional embodiment of the Russian principle of fraternity', quoting 'The free commune has from time immemorial been the Russian people's preferred form of community', and advocated associationism and co-operativism; Dowler says it is 'not obvious' that they meant communalising all property, and some expected a private sphere to remain (hence +1).

culture-before-state.rationale: Dowler: since they idealised autocracy, the pochvenniki 'set politics aside and turned to the ethical restructuring of society', holding that society must take responsibility for its own moral self-improvement and that the state should not control it.

decide-locally.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki wanted the commune and the zemstvo to be separate from central authority 'to preserve local diversity', with local officials elected by universal suffrage; Grigor'ev's localism (mestnost') was dear to him, though Dostoevsky later grew wary of regionalism for fear of separatism.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The 1860 manifesto and Two Camps describe the educated estate as cut off from the people since Peter's reforms and ignorant of them ("it does not know and understand us"); this is the programme's central diagnosis, though it concerns the whole educated estate rather than university graduates as such.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Dowler: Vremia 'recommended that Jews be granted the full rights of citizens', advocated abolishing corporal punishment, and argued that the gentry should have no rights distinct from those of other citizens. Dowler also notes the pochvenniki distrusted law as the basis of social relations, so the answer is +1.

free-trade.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki 'opposed free trade and opted for moderate tariff protection' to protect nascent Russian industry (drawing on Hildebrand's historical school). Strakhov's memoir does list 'freedom of trade' among the liberal principles they supported, so the position is mixed; -1 as the specific economic stance.

freedom-is-self-government-of-desire.rationale: Winter Notes (Dostoevsky, Vremia 1863), ch. 'Baal'/'Brotherhood': 'voluntary, fully conscious, uncompelled self-sacrifice of oneself for all is, in my view, a sign of the highest power of personality, of the highest self-mastery (samoobladanie), of the highest freedom of one's own will'. Freedom is described as self-mastery, not as unrestrained desire. 'Learned' is not stated.

gradual-change.rationale: Dowler reports that contemporaries also called the pochvenniki the 'postepenovtsy' (gradualists): they believed a sudden, rapid transformation would destroy everything quintessentially Russian, and that the national ideal needed to unfold 'step by step along an unhurried and normal path'. Dostoevsky: every society can accommodate only the level of progress to which it has developed. Manifesto: the coming 'overturn' (perevorot) is the fusion of educated society with the national principle, which 'must be accomplished peacefully and in concord'. Dostoevsky's 'A Necessary Literary Explanation' (Vremia, 1863) mocks the progressive critics for whom 'everything is solved at once' ('U menya eto vdrug', says Khlestakov): to arrange 'the happiness of all humanity next week' is for them 'as easy as blowing one's nose'.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Dowler: 'There were no Luddites among the pochvenniki. Science and technology were positive values if harnessed to the correct forms of social and economic organization'; they wished to encourage industrialization and railway building, while condemning capitalism's effects.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The manifesto says Russians cannot fit into any Western form of life, which grew from Europe's own national principles, as one cannot wear clothes cut for someone else, and that Russia must create its own form; this speaks of forms of life in general, political ones included.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Dowler: Native Soil 'was a mid-nineteenth-century Russian reaction against materialism and positivism'; its thinkers were idealists who saw in history the unfolding of a national ideal ('determinism' meaning the unfolding of that ideal, not economic causation), and Vremia was founded to 'counter the growing forces of materialism and utilitarianism'. Economic change is not named as the main historical cause.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki 'were warm advocates of the autocratic ideal' and showed 'enthusiasm for the changes being brought about by the autocracy'; the state 'remained, for them, a constant, the symbol of external order and unity'. Caveat: the monarch they accepted was the actual autocrat, not a merely ceremonial one; the ceremonial limit in the statement is not stated.

morality-needs-religion.rationale: Scanlan (review): Dostoevsky 'grounds ethics in his beliefs'; 'if you were to destroy in humanity the belief in its own immortality, not only love but every vital force for the continuation of earthly life would at once dry up'. Dowler, however, notes the religious motif 'remained suppressed' in Vremia's pochvennichestvo; Dostoevsky's religious grounding is later and fuller. Hence +1, not +2.

municipal-property.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki wanted the free commune restored as 'the Russian people's preferred form of community' and as the basis of an economy of association, with every peasant secured a plot against proletarianization. Caveat: Dowler adds it 'is not obvious ... that moral union with the people meant for them the communalization of all property' and that 'there is even some suggestion that they expected a sphere of private property to continue'.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Dowler: 'They rejected both industrial capitalism and industrial socialism in favour of more libertarian forms of associationism, and co-operativism in agriculture and industry.' Capitalism and the socialism it spawned were seen as mechanistic, exploitative and antithetical to Russian organic life (Dostoevsky's 'socialist anthill'). Dowler's term is 'socialism'; communism is read as its Western form. Dostoevsky's Winter Notes (Vremia, 1863) attacks both the Western bourgeois order ('the bourgeois prospers, pays terribly for his prosperity and fears everything') and the French socialist formula of brotherhood by calculation ('each for all and all for each' assigned by weighing who has earned what).

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Dowler: 'As the group most favoured in the past, the gentry was morally obligated to take the initiative in breaking down class barriers, to further the education of the masses, and, most importantly, to reject the arrogance of learning.' The duty is put on the gentry/educated rather than 'the wealthy' as such.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki accepted autocracy and 'set politics aside'; 'The state remained, for them, a constant, the symbol of external order and unity', while society grew organically. Nothing is said about parties or a nonpartisan office; the state as unifying symbol is the stated element.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki, like the Slavophiles, held the Russian character 'profoundly apolitical', and thought that 'the involvement of society in political affairs through the introduction of constitutionalism violated the very nature of Russians'; they were warm advocates of autocracy. They did want elected zemstva at the local level.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki wanted the zemstvo elected and 'completely free of bureaucratic interference', 'the fullest participation of the peasantry in all the new reform institutions' (zemstvo, jury duty) and the commune resuming 'its traditional role in local self-government'; 'Society had to take responsibility not only for its own administration but also for its moral self-improvement.' These concern local public affairs and institutions, not direct democracy as such.

party-controls-media.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki held that publicity (glasnost') - 'freedom of speech, of the press, and of conscience' - was essential, and opposed state interference in society's affairs; Strakhov lists freedom of thought and speech among the principles they supported.

person-over-state.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki 'attached an overriding significance to personality and were deeply suspicious of anything that imposed restrictions on the development of the individual', held that 'the self-realization of the individual was the prerequisite of national fulfilment', and opposed state control of education and bureaucratic intrusion into society; 'the whole endeavour was profoundly humanistic'. No stated rule against treating persons as tools of collective goals beyond this.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Strakhov, quoted by Dowler, said the pochvenniki stopped 'at pure liberalism, that is, at that doctrine which least of all agrees with the idea of forcible upheaval' and seeks changes 'by means of conviction and persuasion only'. Dowler adds that they rejected 'revolutionary compulsion' to transform society. No text discusses violence in general, hence -1.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The manifesto calls for a form of life of Russia's own, taken from its soil and the popular spirit, and Hudspith describes the movement as grounded in the native soil; it also keeps Western learning, so the answer is strong but not exclusive.

property-franchise.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki held that the zemstvo should be 'democratically elected' and local officials chosen 'by unrestricted universal suffrage'; Vremia (Dec. 1862) 'strongly opposed' Katkov's plan for a high property qualification in zemstvo elections, which would give political rights only to the wealthy.

racial-franchise.rationale: Dowler: Vremia 'recommended that Jews be granted the full rights of citizens', defending them against Aksakov's Den' in 'the Christian spirit of peace, love and concord', and wanted local officials elected 'by unrestricted universal suffrage'. The sources do not discuss ethnic voting rules as such; the Jewish citizenship plank and universal suffrage are the stated positions.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Dowler: Grigor'ev 'reaffirmed the romantic conviction that immediately felt experience was superior to abstract reasoning as the basis of thought and action'; the pochvenniki's thought shifted 'from the abstract and general to the concrete and particular and from the universal truths of reason to the relative truths of historical experience'. Dowler adds that Vremia played down Orthodoxy (the religious motif 'remained suppressed'), so faith itself is not set above reason in so many words; hence -1.

religion-illusion.rationale: Dowler: Native Soil was a reaction against the materialism and atheism of the radical intelligentsia; Scanlan (review): 'Man does not live by bread alone' – Dostoevsky stresses 'that we are not just matter but spirit'. Neither source states the statement's claim directly; both place pochvennichestvo against reducing religion to comfort for material suffering.

religious-nation.rationale: Dowler: for the pochvenniki 'their conception of nationality was more psychological than religious'; Orthodoxy was 'one of the components' and 'one of [the national character's] expressions but not their source'. Vremia defended the Jews against Aksakov's demand that they be excluded from national life unless Orthodox.

restore-past-order.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki opposed a return to the pre-Petrine order, accepted Westernism as a necessary facet of Russian development, and Dostoevsky deplored a conservatism that 'blindly adhered to outmoded forms'. They wanted the national ideal to develop further, not a lost order restored (though they wished to restore the free commune). Manifesto: the Petrine reform is not to be undone: 'the reconciliation of the followers of Peter's reform with the national principle has become a necessity' and the programme concerns 'the reconciliation of civilization with the national principle'. 'Two Camps of Theorists' (Vremia, 1862) rejects the Slavophile return to pre-Petrine Rus' too: 'there was enough falsehood and sham in pre-Petrine Rus', especially in the Moscow period' (falsehood in social relations, religiosity and family life), while calling for the educated to reunite with the people.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Two Camps faults both Westernisers and Slavophiles for judging life by their theory and says theory must submit to the strict check of life's facts; this is said of theories of the people, not of policy as such.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Dowler (ch. 6) writes of the pochvenniki: 'revolutionary change was anathema to them because it imposed ideas and institutions on a society unprepared to receive them. Revolutions invariably destroyed more than their results justified.' They are described as gradualists who wanted change to come naturally, step by step.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Dowler: articles in Vremia 'deplored the egoism and narrowness of the bourgeois ideal'; the pochvenniki's anti-capitalism arose from the view that Western bourgeois life was mechanistic, atomizing and egoistic. No text addresses self-interest as a general moral question.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Dowler: Vremia defended women's emancipation as 'the moral equality of women', so that 'the feudal ideal of chivalry' would give way 'to the love and respect of equals', without diminishing marital duty. No text discusses authority in marriage directly, hence +1.

simple-living.rationale: Dowler: a Vremia political review (Oct. 1861), expounding Proudhon, told Russians to 'devote themselves to quiet industry and voluntarily submit to the law of poverty', distinguishing natural poverty from destitution; the proper end of man was spiritual satisfaction, not material prosperity. The author also said Russia had to increase its labour, so the line is moderate.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Dowler: for the pochvenniki change 'was inevitable and desirable but was legitimate only when it took place within the constraints of tradition'; Dostoevsky defined true conservatism in 1862 as defending 'everything reasonable in the past' while examining every new need. They also attacked conservatism that blindly clung to outmoded forms, so respect for institutions is conditional (+1, not +2).

state-finances-worker-businesses.rationale: Dowler: since the historical form of production in Russia was association, the pochvenniki held that 'the natural form for Russian industrialization was the artel'' (the workers' cooperative); Vremia 'urged the government to extend credit to cottage enterprises and to encourage the co-operative purchasing of raw materials ... through village associations'. State credit to cooperative producers is stated; a general state-financed worker-ownership programme is not, and Vremia made no 'comprehensive scheme' (Dowler).

state-harmful.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki 'were warm advocates of the autocratic ideal'; the state 'remained, for them, a constant, the symbol of external order and unity', although they wanted the sphere of society (the land) kept apart from it.

students-direct-own-learning.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki found their educational ideal in Tolstoy's Yasnaya Polyana journal, whose 'philosophy of education was based on the idea of the removal of all constraint on the student', with the student given 'time and liberty to develop his unique abilities'; Vremia 'adopted' these ideas 'as its own'.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Dowler/Strakhov: the pochvenniki stopped at 'pure liberalism', 'the faith that the absence of compulsory measures leads to the best results', supporting freedom of thought and speech, and rejected 'state intervention to preserve' the order as well as revolutionary compulsion; glasnost (freedom of speech and the press) was 'essential'. No passage addresses suppression of opposition parties as such.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Dowler: 'In order to protect nascent Russian industry from world competition, the pochvenniki, again drawing on contemporary German economic theory, opposed free trade and opted for moderate tariff protection.'

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Hudspith on Winter Notes: Dostoevskii 'sees industry and scientific progress as being virtually deified, particularly at the second World Exhibition, which seemed to him to be frighteningly arrogant'; in the text itself the Crystal Palace is Baal, and 'much eternal spiritual resistance and denial' is needed 'not to bow to the fact'. Dowler adds that the pochvenniki still wanted Western technology (railways, science in agriculture) adopted, so -1, not -2.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Dowler: the pochvenniki 'had hoped ... to infuse the traditional forms of social cohesiveness with the latest advances of science and technology', which Dowler calls 'in the most practical terms ... what Dostoevsky meant by the reconciliation of civilization with the national principles'.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Dowler: for the pochvenniki 'the normal development of a nation depended on strict adherence to its traditions and to the roots of its unique existence'; 'The pochvenniki therefore excluded violent breaks in the continuity of the historical life of the nation. The whole of the past was contained in the present and would direct the future.' They took Peter's reforms as part of that organic development, unlike the Slavophiles.

worker-ownership.rationale: Dowler: since the historical form of production in Russia was association, the pochvenniki argued that 'the natural form for Russian industrialization was the artel'' and favoured co-operative industrial enterprises and co-operativism in agriculture and industry. Dowler cautions that Vremia was not an economic journal and its economic contributions 'were not always consistent'.

missingStatements.text: The educated classes should seek cultural unity with ordinary people.
missingStatements.rationale: The movement's defining aim is the merging of educated society with the people's culture, stated in the manifesto and in Two Camps.

quotes.text: Этот переворот есть слитие образованности и ее представителей с началом народным
мы возвратились самым делом на почву народности, соединились с нашим земством

scope: The programme of Vremya (1861-63) and Epokha (1864-65), the journals of Fyodor and Mikhail Dostoevsky with Apollon Grigor'ev and Nikolai Strakhov, as defining sources (Chances, Dowler, Hudspith, Alekseeva) call it pochvennichestvo, 'native soil': a course midway between Slavophilism and Westernism, built on reconciling the educated estate with the narod. Its core texts are Dostoevsky's 1860 announcement of Vremya and his 1862 article Two Camps of Theorists, with his other writing of 1860-65. It excludes the Slavophile and Westernizer camps it stood between, later Russian nationalism, Dostoevsky's later Diary of a Writer, and twentieth-century 'village prose' writers also called pochvenniki. Dowler's account of Native Soil conservatism is used only for what it attributes to the pochvenniki as a body.
